title: Maipo Valley
description: Santiago's valley: the historic home of Chilean Cabernet Sauvignon, at the foot of the Andes.
L: The Maipo Valley surrounds Chile's capital, Santiago, in the north of the Central Valley. It stretches from the Andes in the east toward the Coastal Range in the west, following the Maipo river. It's small by Chilean standards, about 11,000 hectares, but historically the most important for fine red wine.
Around Santiago, along the Maipo river

Maipo has a warm, dry Mediterranean climate: hot summers, mild winters, rain mostly in winter. Cool air flows down from the Andes at night, giving a big day and night swing. Irrigation from the Maipo river, fed by Andean snowmelt, is essential. Like all Chile, it's free of phylloxera, so vines are ungrafted.
What cools the Maipo Valley at night?
Cold air flowing down from the Andes
Mountain air drains into the valley.

In the mid-19th century, wealthy Chilean families, inspired by Bordeaux, brought French grapes, mostly before phylloxera reached Europe's vineyards. They founded estates near Santiago, like Cousiño Macul, 1856, Santa Rita, 1880, and Concha y Toro, 1883, now Chile's largest wine company. Chilean Cabernet's reputation began here.

Cabernet Sauvignon is Maipo's signature: ripe blackcurrant and cherry, often with a distinctive mint or eucalyptus note, firm but ripe tannins and fresh acidity. Many Chilean icon wines, like Almaviva, a Concha y Toro and Mouton Rothschild partnership, and Don Melchor, are Maipo Cabernets.

Carmenère, brought from Bordeaux in the 19th century, was mixed with Merlot for over a century. In 1994, French ampelographer Jean-Michel Boursiquot identified it. It needs a long, warm season; in Maipo it gives dark fruit, spice and soft tannins, with a green pepper note if unripe. Merlot, Syrah and Cabernet Franc are also grown.
The mint note in Maipo Cabernet is linked by some to eucalyptus trees nearby and by others to the grape's own compounds.
Cabernet Sauvignon is Maipo's signature, often minty
Icons like Almaviva and Don Melchor are Maipo Cabernets

Alto Maipo, upper Maipo, is the eastern part of the valley, in the Andean foothills, at about 600 to 900 m. Areas include Puente Alto, Pirque and Buin. It's cooler than the valley floor, with strong mountain breezes and a big day and night swing.

Soils are alluvial, with stones, gravel and clay, washed down from the Andes by the Maipo river. They drain well and limit vigour. Alto Maipo Cabernet is more structured and elegant than the valley floor's, with blackcurrant, mint, graphite and fine tannins. It's often compared with Bordeaux's Left Bank.
Why is Alto Maipo Cabernet more structured than valley floor Cabernet?
Cooler foothill sites and stony soils

Puente Alto, on an ancient river terrace, is home to some of Chile's most famous Cabernet vineyards: Don Melchor's vineyard, Almaviva and Viñedo Chadwick. Viñedo Chadwick topped a 2004 Berlin tasting, a Chilean version of the Judgment of Paris, ahead of top Bordeaux.

Labels show the grape, the valley, like Valle del Maipo, and sometimes Alto Maipo, Costa, Entre Cordilleras or Andes, descriptors added in 2011 to show position. Chile requires 85% of a named grape, valley and vintage. Reserva and Gran Reserva indicate minimum alcohol, and Gran Reserva some oak, but rules are loose.
Valley plus Andes, Costa or Entre Cordilleras

Maipo Cabernet suits grilled beef, lamb and Chilean dishes like pastel de choclo, a corn and beef pie, and asado. Carmenère suits spicy dishes, grilled pork and dishes with roasted peppers. Serve at 16 to 18 degrees. Top Maipo Cabernet ages 10 to 20 years.
